title: The Red Convertible
author: Louise Erdrich
source: Love Medicine / The Red Convertible: Selected and New Stories (1984)
citation: Erdrich, Louise. 'The Red Convertible.' Love Medicine, Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1984.

sections.heading: The Red Convertible (Complete Narrative Selection)

epigraph.quote: The car was red, a red Oldsmobile... It was the purest summer of our youth.

paragraphs: I was the first one to drive a convertible on my reservation. And of course it was red, a red Oldsmobile, large and sleek, with seats like soft red sofas. My brother Henry Junior and I bought it together with the money I had earned washing dishes and managing the Joliet cafe.

We bought it in the summer of 1970. We saw it sitting on a used-car lot in Minneapolis, red and gleaming under the halogen lights. The minute we bought it, we didn't even go back home to the reservation. We just drove. We drove west across North Dakota, through Montana, into Idaho and Washington, all the way to Alaska and back. We picked up a hitchhiker named Susy with long hair down to her ankles, and lived on cold pinto beans and fresh river trout. It was the purest summer of our youth.

Then Henry was drafted. When he returned from Vietnam three years later, after being held prisoner in a camp, he wasn't the same brother. He had grown quiet, jumpy, like a coiled spring waiting to snap. He would sit for hours staring at the color television with his jaw clenched, barely speaking to our mother or me. The warm, laughing brother who had shared the red Oldsmobile was gone, replaced by a ghost who lived in terror.

To try to bring him back, I took a hammer and deliberately beat up the front bumper and radiator of the convertible, tearing the upholstery and spraying dirt into the engine. I wanted Henry to get mad enough to fix it. When he saw the ruined car, he was furious: 'Lyman, you don't treat a car like this!' He rolled up his sleeves and worked on the convertible day and night for six weeks, replacing the alternator, tuning the engine, polishing the paint until it shone like blood.

When it was finished, Henry invited me to drive down to the Red River in the spring thaw. We parked on the high embankment, listening to the roaring brown water swirling with giant ice floes. Henry suddenly stood up and started dancing in his heavy boots, laughing wildly in the cold wind. 'You can have the convertible, Lyman!' he shouted over the roar of the river. 'It's yours!'

Before I could stop him, Henry walked down to the edge of the river and stepped into the raging water. 'My boots are filling up,' he said quietly as the current caught him. The muddy water dragged him under, and he was swept away beneath the ice.

I sat on the embankment until dusk. Then I started up the red Oldsmobile, put it in gear, turned the headlights on bright, and let it roll down the muddy bank into the river. The headlights cut through the dark swirling water until the current swallowed them whole.
